title: How Canada Is Governed
subtitle: Federal state, parliamentary democracy and the three parts of Parliament

questions.question: What are the three key facts about Canada's system of government?
options: It is a republic, a democracy and a union
It is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy
It is a confederation, a presidency and a monarchy
It is a dominion, a colony and a kingdom
questions.explanation: There are three key facts about Canada's system of government: our country is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy.
questions.ref: Discover Canada, How Canadians Govern Themselves (p. 28)

questions.question: In which document were the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments defined in 1867?
options: The Charter of Rights and Freedoms
The British North America Act, now the Constitution Act, 1867
questions.explanation: The responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments were defined in 1867 in the British North America Act, now known as the Constitution Act, 1867.

questions.question: Which of the following is a responsibility of the federal government?
options: National defence, foreign policy, currency and citizenship
questions.explanation: The federal government handles matters of national and international concern: defence, foreign policy, interprovincial trade and communications, currency, navigation, criminal law and citizenship.

questions.question: Which of the following is a provincial responsibility?
options: Education, health care, natural resources and highways
questions.explanation: The provinces are responsible for municipal government, education, health, natural resources, property and civil rights, and highways.

questions.question: Over which two areas do the federal government and the provinces share jurisdiction?
questions.explanation: The federal government and the provinces share jurisdiction over agriculture and immigration. The responsibilities table also lists the environment as shared.

questions.question: In Canada's parliamentary democracy, what are elected representatives responsible for?
options: Passing laws, approving and monitoring expenditures, and keeping the government accountable
questions.explanation: The people elect members to the House of Commons and to provincial and territorial legislatures. These representatives pass laws, approve and monitor expenditures, and keep the government accountable.

questions.question: What are the three parts of Parliament?
options: The Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the Supreme Court
The Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons
The Governor General, the Premier and the Mayor
The House of Commons, the Senate and the Cabinet
questions.explanation: Parliament has three parts: the Sovereign (King or Queen), the Senate and the House of Commons. Provincial legislatures comprise the Lieutenant Governor and the elected Assembly.

questions.question: How are Senators chosen?
options: Elected by voters every four years
Appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister
questions.explanation: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister and serve until age 75.

questions.question: Until what age do Senators serve?
questions.explanation: Senators serve until age 75.

questions.question: How are members of Parliament chosen?
options: They are appointed by the United Nations
They are chosen by the provincial premiers
They are elected by voters in their local constituency (riding)
They are elected by landowners and police chiefs
questions.explanation: This is a sample question from the guide. The House of Commons is the representative chamber, made up of members of Parliament elected by the people, traditionally every four years.

questions.question: What must happen before a bill can become law in Canada?
options: It must be approved by the Supreme Court
It must be passed by both the House of Commons and the Senate and receive royal assent
It must be approved in a national referendum
It must be signed by all provincial premiers
questions.explanation: No bill can become law until it has been passed by both chambers and has received royal assent, granted by the Governor General on behalf of the Sovereign.

questions.question: What does it mean for Cabinet ministers to retain the "confidence of the House"?
options: They must be liked by the Governor General
They must keep the support of the elected representatives, and resign if defeated in a non-confidence vote
They must win re-election every year
They must be approved by the Senate
questions.explanation: Cabinet ministers are responsible to the elected representatives, which means they must retain the confidence of the House and have to resign if they are defeated in a non-confidence vote.

questions.question: Who selects the Cabinet ministers and is responsible for the operations and policy of the government?
questions.explanation: In the federal government the Prime Minister selects the Cabinet ministers and is responsible for the operations and policy of the government.

questions.question: Members of a provincial legislature may be called MLAs, MNAs, MPPs or MHAs. What does MPP stand for?
questions.explanation: Depending on the province, members are called members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs), National Assembly (MNAs, in Quebec), Provincial Parliament (MPPs, in Ontario) or House of Assembly (MHAs, in Newfoundland and Labrador).

questions.question: What does federalism allow provinces to do?
options: Adopt policies tailored to their own populations and experiment with new ideas
questions.explanation: Federalism allows different provinces to adopt policies tailored to their own populations, and gives provinces the flexibility to experiment with new ideas and policies.

questions.question: True or false: The three northern territories have the same status as provinces.
questions.explanation: False. The three northern territories, which have small populations, do not have the status of provinces, but their governments and assemblies carry out many of the same functions.

questions.question: True or false: Every province has its own elected Legislative Assembly, like the House of Commons in Ottawa.
questions.explanation: True. Every province has its own elected Legislative Assembly, like the House of Commons in Ottawa.

questions.question: True or false: Both the House of Commons and the Senate consider and review bills.
questions.explanation: True. Both the House of Commons and the Senate consider and review bills (proposals for new laws).

questions.question: Members of the House of Commons are traditionally elected how often?
questions.explanation: The House of Commons is made up of members of Parliament elected by the people, traditionally every four years.

questions.question: What are the four levels of government mentioned in the guide?
questions.explanation: There are federal, provincial, territorial and municipal governments in Canada. The study question "What are the three levels of government?" is usually answered: federal, provincial/territorial and municipal (local).
